chunks.content:
Entra ID every time to know whether a session is still allowed. They can locally evaluate key
Conditional Access policies because Entra has already synchronized the relevant policy signals
into the workload. This then lets them detect changes in conditions like location and risk and
enforce CAE immediately.
Client capabilities
Without CAE, clients like Outlook, Teams and OneDrive can replay a user's access token from
their cache idx_6696597b as long as it is not expired. With CAE, a token can be rejected idx_57132d05 even if it is not
expired. A mechanism idx_5bc4470e called claim challenge is used to inform a client to bypass its cache. The
latest versions of Outlook, Teams and OneDrive support claim challenge.
With CAE, access tokens no longer rely on short, fixed lifetimes. CAE-capable clients use real-
time policy and risk evaluation, so tokens can safely last up to 28 hours. Security comes from
instant revocation when conditions change and not from expiring tokens. Clients that aren't
CAE-aware continue using the traditional 1-hour token lifetime or any custom lifetime
configured using Configurable Token Lifetime settings.
Securing workload identities
In addition to user and sign-in risk, Microsoft Entra ID Protection also helps in securing
workload idx_a31271bf identities helping detect, investigate, and remediate risks related to applications and
service idx_51137d35 principals. A workload identity is an identity assigned to an application and allows it
to access resources. Unlike a user account, a workload identity cannot perform MFA and often
does not have a lifecycle. But they do need a secure location to store their credentials or secrets.
Due to this, they are more vulnerable to attacks. To make use of the workload identity risk
report, the following pre-requisites must be met.
Administrator should have the Security Administrator, Security Operator, or
Security Reader role assigned
To use risk as a condition while creating Conditional Access policies, the Conditional
Access Administrator role must be assigned
To take action on risky workload identities using risk based Conditional Access
policies, you must have a Workload Identities Premium license

In today's world, we use identities at work, at home, and across various devices and
applications. These identities represent us as individuals and are made up of everything we do
or experience, such as online shopping, booking a cab, or ordering dinner. Our identities and
digital interactions depend on many applications to which we grant access to our data. Often,
we are not aware which applications have access to which pieces of our personal information.
In the enterprise world, collaboration with customers and partners requires orchestration to
exchange information. This introduces the risk of identity theft and data breaches.
Decentralized identities are digital identities that are owned and controlled by individuals,
giving them greater control over which application has access to which of their personal data.
Using decentralized technologies, users can create, manage, and share their identity securely
with full privacy and autonomy. This approach reduces reliance on traditional identity systems
that store sensitive information in centralized databases, which can be vulnerable to data
breaches or misuse. We need decentralized identities to empower people with more control
over their personal information, enhance privacy, reduce identity theft, and make it easier to
verify identity across different organizations and platforms without sharing excess data.
In this chapter, we will cover:

Introduction to decentralized identities
Decentralized identities represent a significant shift from traditional, centralized identity
management systems. In conventional models, identity data such as usernames, passwords,
and personal information is stored and managed by a central authority—typically an
organization or service provider. This centralization makes sensitive data a prime target for
cyberattacks idx_6928dceb and puts users at risk of identity theft, loss of privacy, and unauthorized access. In
contrast, decentralized identities (DIDs) empower individuals to own, control, and manage
their digital identity without relying on a single provider or intermediary.

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 338
chunks.content:
At the core of idx_d2ebe216 decentralized identity is the concept of self-sovereign identity (SSI), where
individuals have full ownership and autonomy over their personal data. Rather than having
identity information scattered across multiple organizations, users create and manage a digital
identity that is stored in a secure digital wallet—often on their own device. This wallet can
contain various verifiable credentials, such as government-issued IDs, educational certificates,
or employment records, which are cryptographically signed by trusted issuers. When a user
needs to prove their identity, they can selectively share only the necessary credentials, thereby
minimizing data exposure and enhancing privacy.
Decentralized identities leverage distributed ledger technologies, such as blockchains, to
provide a secure and tamper-evident infrastructure for managing identity data. Blockchains
are used to anchor decentralized identifiers, which are unique, persistent identifiers created
and controlled by the user. Unlike traditional identifiers, decentralized identifiers are not
dependent on any central registry, authority, or intermediary. This design allows for greater
interoperability between systems and organizations, making it easier for users to interact
across different platforms without repeatedly creating new identities or sharing sensitive
information unnecessarily.
One of the key benefits of decentralized identities is enhanced privacy. With traditional
identity systems, users often have little visibility into which organizations have access to their
personal information or how that data is being used. DIDs give users granular control over
their data, allowing them to grant or revoke access as needed. For example, instead of
providing a full copy of a driver's license to verify age, a user could share only a cryptographic
proof that they are over a certain age, without revealing their exact birthdate or other personal
details.
Security is another major advantage. Since identity data is not stored in a single, centralized
location, the risk of large-scale data breaches is significantly reduced. In decentralized systems,
even if one credential issuer is compromised, the user's other credentials remain secure, as
each is independently managed and cryptographically protected. Furthermore, decentralized

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 342
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 342
identities can help prevent identity fraud by enabling real-time verification of credentials and
reducing the reliance on easily stolen or forged information.
Decentralized identities also promote inclusivity and accessibility. Individuals who lack
traditional identity documents or live in regions with limited infrastructure can create digital
identities that are recognized globally. This enables access to services such as banking,
healthcare, and education, regardless of geographic location or socioeconomic status. The
portability of decentralized identities means users can carry their credentials across borders
and platforms, fostering seamless digital interactions in an increasingly connected world.
Decentralized identities idx_2ca675b2 offer a transformative approach to digital identity management. By
shifting control from centralized authorities to individuals, DIDs enhance privacy, security,
and user autonomy. They reduce the risks associated with data breaches and identity theft,
streamline the verification process, and open up opportunities for people who are underserved
by traditional systems. As technology and standards continue to evolve, decentralized
identities are poised to become a cornerstone of secure, user-centric digital ecosystems.
A digital identity represents who a person is in a digital space. Verifiable credentials help prove
specific claims about that person when needed.
Introduction to verifiable credentials
Verifiable credentials are a foundational concept in the emerging landscape of decentralized
identity systems. They idx_33bf09b4 provide a secure, privacy-preserving, and interoperable way to prove
attributes, qualifications, or claims about an individual, organization, or device in the digital
world. Unlike traditional credentials, such as plastic ID cards or paper certificates, verifiable
credentials are digitally signed and can be presented, validated, and revoked with
cryptographic assurance. This approach not only streamlines the process of sharing and
verifying information but also gives individuals greater control over their personal data,
reducing the risk of identity theft, fraud, and data misuse.
At their core, verifiable credentials are digital statements made by a trusted issuer about a
person. These statements, or claims, can represent a wide range of information—from
government-issued identification and academic qualifications to professional licenses and
memberships. Each credential is composed of three main components: the issuer (who creates
and signs the credential), the subject (the person to whom the credential pertains), and the
verifier (who checks the authenticity of the credential). The credentials themselves are typically
idx_74fcfc41 encoded in a standard data model, such as the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 342
chunks.content:
Verifiable Credentials standard, ensuring interoperability across different platforms and
organizations.
343 Microsoft Entra Verified ID
The lifecycle of a verifiable credential begins when an issuer, such as a university or
government agency, generates a digital credential for a subject. This credential is
cryptographically signed to guarantee its authenticity and integrity. The subject then stores
the credential in a secure digital wallet, often managed on their own device. When the subject
needs to prove a claim—such as their age, educational attainment, or professional status—
they can present the relevant credential to a verifier, such as an employer or service provider.
The verifier checks the digital signature and, if necessary, queries the issuer or a decentralized
ledger to confirm the credential's validity and revocation status.
One of the most idx_bb639eee significant benefits of verifiable credentials is enhanced privacy. Subjects can
choose to share only the minimum amount of information required for a specific transaction,
rather than disclosing their entire identity or sensitive personal details. For example, to prove
eligibility for a senior discount, a user could present a credential that confirms they are over a
certain age without revealing their exact birthdate or other identifying information. This
concept, known as selective disclosure, is enabled by advanced cryptographic techniques such as
zero-knowledge proofs.
Verifiable credentials also foster trust in digital ecosystems by ensuring that credentials can be
independently verified without relying on a single central authority. Because credentials are
digitally signed by trusted issuers and anchored to decentralized identifiers, verifiers can
validate their authenticity in real time. This reduces opportunities for forgery or tampering and
simplifies compliance with regulatory requirements for identity verification, such as Know
Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) regulations. Additionally, revocation
mechanisms allow issuers to invalidate credentials if they are found to be compromised or no
longer valid, further enhancing security and trust.
The applications of verifiable credentials are broad and rapidly expanding. In education, digital
diplomas, and transcripts can be issued as verifiable credentials, allowing graduates to share
their achievements instantly with employers or other institutions. In healthcare, verifiable
credentials can represent professional medical licenses or proof of vaccination status,
streamlining access to services and improving patient privacy. In finance, banks and fintech
companies can use verifiable credentials to onboard customers more efficiently while
maintaining regulatory compliance. Even everyday scenarios, such as age verification for

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 342
chunks.content:
online purchases or access control for events, can benefit from verifiable, privacy-preserving
credentials.
Interoperability is a key consideration in the adoption of verifiable credentials. W3C has
established open standards for verifiable credentials and decentralized identifiers, enabling
seamless idx_aba31ad1 interaction between different identity systems and service providers. Organizations
like the Decentralized Identity Foundation (DIF) and the W3C Credentials Community

chunks.title: masteringmicrosoftentraid
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 344
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 344
Group are driving the development and adoption idx_46cee8fe of these standards, ensuring that verifiable
credentials can be used globally across a variety of platforms and industries.
Despite their promise, verifiable credentials face several challenges. Achieving widespread
adoption requires collaboration among issuers, wallet providers, verifiers, and regulators to
establish trusted ecosystems and governance frameworks. Ensuring usability and accessibility
for all users, including those with limited technical skills or resources, is essential for inclusion.
There are also ongoing discussions about privacy, data protection, and interoperability, as well
as the need for robust mechanisms to handle credential revocation and recovery in case of
device loss or compromise.
Verifiable credentials idx_e9d2e28e represent a transformative step forward in digital identity management.
They empower individuals to control their personal information, reduce reliance on
centralized authorities, and create new possibilities for secure, privacy-preserving interactions
online. As standards mature and adoption grows, verifiable credentials are poised to become a
cornerstone of decentralized, user-centric digital ecosystems, supporting a wide range of
services and enabling trusted digital interactions around the world.
Now that we understand the core concepts, let's look at how digital identity and verifiable
credentials are implemented in Microsoft Entra.
Understanding Microsoft Entra Verified ID
Microsoft Entra Verified ID is a cutting-edge solution designed to enable secure, privacy-
respecting digital idx_c0fe6041 identity verification for individuals and organizations. Built on open
standards such as W3C Verifiable Credentials and Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), Entra
Verified ID empowers users to obtain, manage, and present digital credentials in a trustworthy
and interoperable manner. With Entra Verified ID, organizations can issue digital credentials—
such as proof of employment, educational qualifications, or professional certifications—that
users store securely in their own digital wallets. When users need to verify their identity or
claims, they can selectively disclose only the necessary information to verifiers, maintaining
control over their personal data and enhancing privacy.
Microsoft Entra Verified ID integrates seamlessly with existing identity systems and platforms,
making it easier for businesses to adopt decentralized identity solutions without overhauling
their infrastructure. The platform supports robust security measures, including cryptographic
signatures, and real-time revocation, to ensure that credentials are authentic and up to date.
By removing the need for centralized authorities and enabling user-centric identity
management, Entra Verified ID reduces the risk of fraud, streamlines onboarding, and

controlled, and scalable identity solutions for the modern world.

As can be understood, a new form of identity requires new innovations. Decentralized
identities are made up of five key innovations as shown in the following figure:
Figure 10.1: Decentralized identity
The following points explain each of the components in Figure 10.1:
W3C Decentralized identifiers: Everything starts with a DID that users can create,
own and idx_480ea35e control independently. DIDs are unique identifiers that are linked to
Decentralized Public Key Infrastructure (DPKI). DID documents are JSON
documents that contain public key material, authentication descriptors and service
endpoints.
Trust system: At the core is a trust system that is used to resolve the DIDs. Microsoft
leverages the did:web trust system, which allows trust using a domain's reputation.
Microsoft Authenticator App: This is the user agent or wallet where the users can
store and present their DIDs and Verifiable Credentials.
Microsoft Resolver: This API facilitates the lookup and resolution of a DID utilizing the
did:web method.
Microsoft Entra Verified ID: This is the issuance and verification service that enables
subjects to create, own and present their DIDs. This is the basis of the trust between
issuers, holders and verifiers.

to provide a government identification proof and perform a face check against that as a part of
the verification process. This is particularly useful in cases of remote onboarding and total loss
recovery – when employees have lost all access to their account and need to recover.

Chapter 10 362
Verified ID Face Check
Verified ID Face idx_f09763b8 Check is a security feature designed to enhance the trustworthiness and
integrity of digital identity verification processes. By incorporating biometric authentication,
specifically facial recognition, the Verified ID Face Check ensures that the individual presenting
a verifiable credential is the legitimate owner. The process typically involves prompting the
user to take a real-time selfie, which is then compared against the photo or biometric data
stored in their digital credential or on file with a trusted issuer.
This technology is crucial in preventing identity fraud and impersonation since it makes it
much harder for malicious actors to use stolen or fake credentials. Face Check can be
seamlessly integrated into onboarding workflows, remote access scenarios, or high-value
transactions, providing organizations with a robust layer of assurance. Additionally, it
supports privacy by processing biometric data in compliance with regulations, often ensuring
that sensitive information is not stored or transmitted unnecessarily.
For users, the experience idx_bfe5575e is streamlined and user-friendly, usually requiring only a few
moments to complete. The combination of ease of use and enhanced security makes Verified ID
Face Check an attractive option for enterprises looking to protect both their assets and their
users' identities in a digital-first world.
Enabling Face Check
Face Check idx_cf7df037 can be enabled from within the Microsoft Entra admin center or by using the REST
API. The following are the steps to enable Face Check from the Microsoft Entra admin center:
Sign in to https://entra.microsoft.com as Authentication Policy Administrator.
Navigate to Verified ID | Overview.
Scroll down. Under Add-ons click Turn on. Refer Figure 10.3.
You will have to link an Azure subscription for billing purposes. Select the Subscription,
Resource group, and location and click Validate.
Once validated, click on Turn on as shown in the screenshot below:

Organizations can idx_bdb6e2c0 now require users to perform a Face Check when performing high-value
transactions like resetting passwords, requesting access packages, or accessing critical
resources.
The biometric idx_8b682238 check between the photo and the real time selfie is performed in the cloud using
Azure AI Vision Face API. This service checks for liveness, which means that it ensures that it
is a real person who has captured the picture and that a static 2D picture or video was not used.
The footage is captured on the mobile device and is passed on to Verified ID. Verified ID uses it
to involve Azure AI services. Once processing is complete, the image is discarded. It is not saved
in the Microsoft Authenticator app or any online services. It is also not shared with the site or
service that requested the Face Check. The verifier only gets a likeness match score which is the
percentage of confidence that the Face Check was performed by the same individual whose
picture it is being compared with.
Licensing
There are idx_1de83035 two options for licensing for Face Check:
Pay-as-you-go: Organizations with Microsoft Entra Free, P1 or P2 can pay per face
check verification.
Entra Suite: Organizations with Entra Suite licenses get 8 face checks per seat per
month. These are aggregated at the tenant level. If an organization consumes all of
these, they are charged as per the pay-as-you-go model.
Choose the appropriate model depending on your organization's needs and the licenses it
owns.

Licensing
To use idx_c58ed849 this feature, the organization must have Microsoft Entra ID Governance or Entra Suite
licenses.
Now let's learn how Microsoft Entra Verified ID helps in situations where users lose their
devices and have no way of accessing their accounts.
Account recovery
Most organizations today require users to complete several authentication methods to access
resources. Sometimes situations arise where users lose all access to their authentication
methods. They lose idx_d9676dbc their primary device, and all backup codes are lost. In such cases, self-
service password reset becomes useless as it requires users to provide at least one form of
registered authentication method. This is a bigger problem for passwordless users who have
no self-service options. In most cases, the user must call the helpdesk. The helpdesk must
ensure that the user is who they are claiming to be. Usually, they rely on security questions like
mother's maiden name, pet's name or the street someone grew up on. This process has
inherent risks as this information is easily discoverable in today's social media world. A bad
actor can easily impersonate an employee or, worse, a senior executive.
Microsoft Entra ID Account Recovery addresses these scenarios by enabling users to recover
their accounts using robust identity verification processes. Account recovery differs from
password reset in that password reset assumes that the user has some form of second factor
authentication still available. Account recovery assumes that the user has lost all forms of
authentication and a total loss recovery needs to be performed. It shifts the focus from simple
password reset to comprehensive identity verification and re-onboarding. It leverages Verified
ID to ensure that the person requesting the account recovery is the actual owner of the
account.

369 Microsoft Entra Verified ID
Account recovery follows an identity-centric approach and shifts the focus from something you
know (passwords) and something you have (MFA options) to who you are by using robust ID
proofing mechanisms. Account recovery is treated as employee re-onboarding, where the
organization must re-establish trust in the employee's identity. Leveraging modern
technologies like Verified ID and Face Check, it provides strong assurance of the user identity
during the account recovery process.
It is most suited for scenarios where a user has lost their primary device that has all their
authentication methods or when a security incident has compromised the user's account.
Account recovery is a self-service process that reduces the burden on helpdesk by providing a
secure option for total account recovery. It also improves user experience as they don't have to
wait for the helpdesk to be available to help them.
It integrates with trusted third-party identity verification providers to use government-issued
IDs for user identification and biometric verification. The following picture shows the account
recovery workflow:
Figure 10.16: Account recovery workflow
The recovery idx_2dc0a4e3 workflow consists of four steps.
User is onboarded into the organization. They provide their account identifiers like
usernames or email addresses. They register additional authentication methods like
Microsoft authenticator app or passkeys. They then lose their trusted devices and
hence lose access to their account.
1.

chunks.content:
Chapter 10 370
The user starts the recovery flow and is prompted to upload a government-issued ID
document like a passport or driving license. They are asked to perform a biometric
verification against the ID. This could be a face check that matches a real-time selfie
with the picture on the uploaded ID document.
The user is now trusted as the ID information matches their account.
The user is now issued a Verified ID from their organization that they can store in their
Microsoft Authenticator app and present to Microsoft Entra ID to recover their account.
At this point Entra ID can ask for another Face Check to match the user's selfie with the
profile picture on their Entra ID user object. Users are then guided through account
recovery and registering new authentication methods.
Account recovery in Entra ID also has a special configuration wizard that enables admins to
define recovery requirements, detailing who can recover and which trusted providers can
provide identity proofing services. It is a secure by default feature. It has an evaluation mode
and is very quick to set up.
Microsoft Entra ID P1 is required to enable account recovery.
Account recovery idx_8244d7f7 in Microsoft Entra ID uses government-issued IDs and biometric verification
through a secure, configurable workflow, allowing users to regain access when trusted devices
are lost.
Revoking credentials
Once a user is issued a verifiable credential, it is theirs. However, sometimes organizations may
need to idx_301803e7 revoke credentials in scenarios like employee termination. Microsoft Entra Verified ID
implements the W3C Bitstring Status List, which is a mechanism for publishing the status of
verifiable credentials. When Microsoft Entra Verified ID issues a verified credential, it contains
a claim called credentialStatus, which is where a verified credential has its revocation flag.
Since Microsoft Entra Verified ID does not store verified credentials, the issuer of the credential
needs to have one claim so that the credential can be searched. Only one claim can be indexed.
If this claim does not exist, the credential cannot be revoked because Microsoft Entra Verified
ID cannot find it. This claim is salted and hashed and then stored. Its original value is not
stored.

3.4 373 Microsoft Entra Verified ID
Opting out of Verified ID service
Opting out of Verified ID is the process of resetting the service at your Microsoft Entra tenant
level. This is idx_69c7a8b6 a one-way operation and once complete the organization's Verified ID
environment is reset to defaults. Organizations might choose to do this if they want to enable
new services or reset their existing configuration.
To opt out of the Verified ID service, follow these steps:
Login to https://entra.microsoft.com as Admin user that has the sign key
permission on the Azure Key Vault.
Navigate to Verified ID | Organization settings. Click on Delete all credentials and
reset service.
In the fly out pane, click on Delete & opt out.
When organizations opt out of the Verified ID service, Microsoft deletes the DID keys in Azure
Key Vault. The issuer object, tenant identifier, and all verifiable credentials contracts are also
deleted. Once the idx_6c7efbe6 deletion is complete, the DID cannot be recovered and no operations can be
conducted on it. If organizations want to use the service, they will have to onboard again
which results in the creation of a new environment. The verifiable credentials already issued
continue to exist.
Summary
In this chapter, we explored decentralized identities and verifiable credentials. We covered
how to use the Microsoft Entra Verified ID service, including both quick and advanced setup
methods. The chapter also detailed using Verified ID Face Check for high-assurance identity
verification and explained its integration with entitlement management. Additionally, we
introduced the basics of the new account recovery feature and discussed its applications in
different scenarios. Finally, we learned how to revoke individual verifiable credentials.
